title: Kashmir on a Plate: What the Swiss President Ate at Rashtrapati Bhavan
excerpt: President Droupadi Murmu's October 6 banquet for Guy Parmelin served a Kashmiri-Ladakhi spread — Nadur Kebab, Dum Oluv, Shufta and more — during his three-day India visit.
body:
• President Droupadi Murmu hosted Swiss President Guy Parmelin and First Lady Caroline Parmelin at a state banquet at Rashtrapati Bhavan on October 6, during Parmelin's three-day visit to India (October 5–7).
  • The multi-course menu drew on the cuisines of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh: Za Thuk nettle soup, Nadur Kebab with walnut chutney, Chaman Qaliya, Dum Oluv, Kanna Guchh Pulao, and desserts Shufta, Phirin, and Phaymer — with Kahwa and Gur Gur Chai to drink.
  • Kashmir is often called the 'Switzerland of India,' and the Himalayan menu was a deliberate nod — pairing the food of the Indian Himalayas with the cuisine of the Alps.
  • The visit also carried substance: agreements on migration and mobility, research, and technology transfer, plus trade talks under the India-EFTA Trade and Partnership Agreement. PM Modi separately gifted Parmelin three award-winning Indian cheeses — Gulmarg, Konark, and Yeoor.

A Himalayan menu for the Alpine president

When Swiss President Guy Parmelin sat down to dinner at Rashtrapati Bhavan on October 6, the plate in front of him told a story. President Droupadi Murmu's state banquet for Parmelin and First Lady Caroline Parmelin served a menu drawn entirely from the culinary traditions of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh — a deliberate choice, given that Kashmir is often called the 'Switzerland of India.' The evening paired the food of the Indian Himalayas with the tastes of the Alps, turning a state dinner into an exercise in edible diplomacy.

The multi-course spread, reported by ANI and India Today, opened with Za Thuk — a nourishing Ladakhi wild nettle soup with winter peas, garnished with roasted millet pearls — followed by Lab-In Tsonma, a cheese salad showcasing Ladakh's Labo and Chhurpi, Jammu's Kalari, dried apple, walnuts, and wild capers in a sea buckthorn and honey dressing, served with buckwheat crackers and Ladakhi apricot jam.

From Nadur Kebab to Shufta

The appetisers were the evening's headline acts. Nadur Kebab with Dooy Chetin — lotus stem patties seasoned with Kashmiri spices, served with walnut chutney — sat alongside Kimb Chaat, a Jammu street-food delicacy of boiled taro root, sweet potatoes, and rice-flour crispies with sweetened yoghurt, tamarind, and starfruit, and Jackfruit Phorok, a charcoal-roasted Ladakhi wheat dumpling stuffed with turnip greens.

The main course stayed rooted in Kashmiri Pandit and Ladakhi kitchens: Chaman Qaliya, delicately spiced cottage cheese in a milk-and-turmeric sauce; Haakh, collard greens stewed with mustard oil and asafoetida; Dum Oluv, potatoes cooked with yoghurt, dry ginger, and fennel; Tsok Wangun, baby aubergine in a tangy clove-and-ginger sauce; and Kanna Guchh Pulao, fragrant rice with Kashmiri morels. Sheermal and Katlam breads and a white-radish yoghurt relish rounded out the table.

Dessert was a Kashmiri-Ladakhi trio: Shufta, a rich blend of stewed dry dates, cashew nuts, raisins, and coconut garnished with poppy seeds; Phirin, a saffron-and-cardamom semolina and milk pudding; and Phaymer, a Ladakhi dessert of roasted barley, jaggery, and butter with soft cheese. The beverages — Kashmiri Kahwa, Ladakhi Gur Gur Chai, and wild rose tea — closed the meal.

Food as foreign policy

State banquet menus are never just about feeding guests. By centring the cuisines of J&K and Ladakh, the dinner put two of India's most tourism-potential regions on a global stage — and drew a direct cultural line between the Himalayas and the Alps, between Kashmir's meadows and Switzerland's. It is a well-worn but effective soft-power play: make the guest feel at home by showing them a reflection of their own landscape in yours.

The symbolism extended beyond the table. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who hosted Parmelin for lunch separately, gifted the Swiss president three award-winning Indian cheeses — Gulmarg, a French-style Brie from Mumbai's Eleftheria Cheese that won a Super Gold at the 2026 Mundial do Queijo do Brasil; Konark, a Gold winner at the 2023 World Cheese Awards; and Yeoor, aged nine months. Presenting cheese to the president of Switzerland — a country whose identity is inseparable from cheese — was a confident flex: India's artisanal food scene now competes on the world stage.

The business behind the banquet

The visit carried real weight beyond the menu. Parmelin's three-day trip included agreements on migration and mobility, research cooperation, and technology transfer, with President Murmu highlighting fresh opportunities under the India-European Free Trade Association Trade and Partnership Agreement. She pointed to Swiss companies' footprint in Indian infrastructure — roads, railway bridges, tunnels — and invited them into clean technology and artificial intelligence. The banquet's regional focus was part of the pitch: a reminder that India's economic story now includes its mountains.

What's next

Parmelin's visit wraps on October 7. For the diaspora, the dinner is a reminder of how India's culinary diplomacy has matured — from generic 'Indian food' to region-specific showcases that double as tourism and trade marketing. The next time Kashmir or Ladakh appears on a Swiss supermarket shelf or a Zurich travel itinerary, this dinner will have done some of the work.
